review_material.assessment: The source supports the normalized-friction fits for the viscous-inertial transition. The public control St ranges from 0.01 to 300. The common fixed condition K_phi = J + 0.1 I^2 = 0.065 is supported by the two simulation runs at St=0.65 and 206.5. The derived relations J(St)=0.065/(1+0.1 St), K_mu(St)=0.065*(1+alpha_mu St)/(1+0.1 St), and r(St)=1+a_mu*sqrt(K_mu(St)) are consistent with the source equations and fits. The private branch mu_f=0.15 uses a_mu=14.3 and alpha_mu=0.029; the alternate branch mu_f=0.80 uses a_mu=26.5 and alpha_mu=0.00875. All constants are anchored. The case is authoring-ready.

mechanisms.statement: The macroscopic friction coefficient mu is governed by a single dimensionless number K_mu = J + alpha_mu I^2, with alpha_mu = 1/St_{v->i}^mu, and the normalized friction r = mu/mu_c follows r = 1 + a_mu * sqrt(K_mu). The packing fraction phi follows phi = phi_c (1 - a_phi sqrt(K_phi)) with K_phi = J + alpha_phi I^2 and alpha_phi = 0.1.

review_material.paper_scope: Particle-resolved simulations of dense frictional suspensions undergoing the viscous-inertial transition using pressure-imposed rheology. The study varies fluid viscosity, shear rate, and granular pressure, and examines the effect of interparticle friction on the transition. The key findings are the distinct scalings of packing fraction phi and macroscopic friction mu, governed by different alpha values, and the role of tangential contact and lubrication forces.

source_ambiguities.statement: The paper reports alpha_mu = 0.029 for mu_f=0.15 in the main text (line 252) and in Table 1 (line 358). However, the abstract and introduction mention alpha_mu = 0.0088 for the experiments of Tapia et al. (line 133). The numerical value for the reference case is 0.029, which is used here.
